ownership_reason: Only the gold reads the stored checksum and holds the checksum of the block; hops 1-4 see the header and the historic (signed) checksum and get back one boolean, from which the unsigned sum cannot be recovered. The convention is pinned outside the gold: TarUtils.computeCheckSum computes the checksum of a tar header as the sum of BYTE_MASK & element; TarArchiveEntry.writeEntryHeader fills the checksum field with eight spaces and stores that sum with formatCheckSumOctalBytes; the facade's javadoc states the checksum is the sum of the unsigned byte values with the eight checksum bytes taken as spaces, that some historic implementations treated bytes as signed, and that the stored checksum is also accepted when it is greater than the computed unsigned checksum; hop 2 documents the historic checksum as the signed sum. Passing tests: headers written by writeEntryHeader are accepted (TarArchiveEntryTest testTarFileWithFSRoot), a header with high bytes whose stored checksum is its unsigned sum is accepted (TarArchiveInputStreamTest datePriorToEpochInGNUFormat), and TarUtilsTest testVerifyHeaderCheckSum and ArchiveStreamFactoryTest aiffFilesAreNoTARs pass. On the trigger's block the stored checksum is 0 and the checksum of the block is 111371, so the block is not a tar header; summing the signed bytes gives -245 and accepts it.
